items.title: The Gulf Stream keeps the UK warmer than it would otherwise be
items.claim: How much does the Gulf Stream warm Britain?

options.text: Not at all — UK climate is determined by latitude alone
Comparison with similar-latitude locations (Calgary, Labrador) suggests the wider North Atlantic Current warms western Europe by around 5-10°C above what latitude would predict
By around 30°C — without it Britain would be like Antarctica

items.reveal:
The Gulf Stream is the western boundary current of the North Atlantic gyre; it widens north of Cape Hatteras into the North Atlantic Current. Prevailing westerlies carry the warm air onto western Europe.

Richard Seager and colleagues (2002) argued that latitude differences and atmospheric heat transport from west to east are at least as important as the ocean current itself. The popular 'Gulf Stream alone keeps Britain warm' line oversimplifies.

The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) has weakened by an estimated 15% since the mid-20th century (Caesar et al., 2018, 2021).
items.why: Climate is the product of multiple systems. Single-cause stories (it's the Gulf Stream!) miss how ocean and atmosphere together shape regional temperature.

items.title: Coral reefs cover under 1% of the ocean but host around 25% of marine species
items.claim: What proportion of marine biodiversity do coral reefs support?

options.text: Around 25% of all marine species live on coral reefs, which cover less than 1% of the ocean floor — perhaps the most concentrated biodiversity hotspot on Earth
Coral reefs support only the species visible to divers

items.reveal:
Reefs occupy around 284,000 km² globally — under 0.1% of the ocean. The Great Barrier Reef is 2,300 km long. Species counts: around 4,000 fish species, 800 reef-building coral species, plus uncounted invertebrates.

Mass bleaching events (1998, 2010, 2014-17, 2024) have hit major reef systems. The Great Barrier Reef has experienced bleaching in 2016, 2017, 2020, 2022 and 2024. Some 50% of shallow corals on the GBR died in the 2016 event.

Reefs also provide coastal protection, fisheries and tourism value estimated at hundreds of billions of dollars annually.
items.why: Conservation priorities follow concentration. A small fraction of the planet holds an outsized share of biodiversity — losing reefs means losing whole ecosystems, not just iconic species.

items.title: The Amazon used to flow the other way
items.claim: Today the Amazon flows from the Andes east into the Atlantic. What did it do before the Andes rose?

options.text: It always flowed east; the basin's shape has been stable for 100 million years
It drained westward into the Pacific until the Andes rose and reversed the gradient around 10 million years ago
It split into two systems, one east and one west, until tectonic activity merged them
It originally flowed north into the Caribbean

items.reveal:
Through the Cretaceous and early Cenozoic, the proto-Amazon drained westward into the Pacific. As the Andes uplifted from around 65 Ma but accelerated after 23 Ma, the western outlet was blocked. A vast inland wetland system (the Pebas system) developed in what is now western Amazonia.

By roughly 10-11 Ma, the river had cut through to the Atlantic and reversed. Hoorn et al. (Science, 2010) reconstructed the history from sediment cores.
items.why: Rivers feel like fixed features of geography. They are the temporary result of whatever tectonic surface is currently tilting. Change the tilt, change the flow.
